name: Phoenician circumnavigation of Africa
who: Phoenician crews sent by the pharaoh Necho II
dates_text: sometime between 610 and 594 BC, three years
why: Known only from Herodotus, writing about 150 years later from oral tradition. His sceptical remark that the sailors had the sun on their right is often read as a sign of truth, but historians such as Lloyd and Haywood doubt the voyage could be provisioned or sailed as described.
return_note: Herodotus says they came back to Egypt by the Pillars of Heracles in the third year.

name: Scylax down the Indus and round Arabia
who: Scylax of Caryanda, for Darius I of Persia
dates_text: late 6th century BC; Herodotus says thirty months
why: Herodotus is the only narrative source and Scylax's own book is lost. Its starting city has never been securely identified and the river is described flowing the wrong way, so some commentators doubt the voyage happened; others read Caspatyrus as Peshawar.
return_note: Herodotus has the fleet reach the head of the Red Sea after thirty months.

name: Euthymenes down the coast of West Africa
who: Euthymenes of Massalia
why: His account is lost; it survives only second-hand in Plutarch and Seneca, who refuted it. He described a great river that made the sea fresh at its mouth, with wildlife like the Nile's, and took it for the Nile; it may have been the Senegal, but where he reached is guesswork.
return_note: He wrote an account of the voyage, so he came home, but nothing about the return survives.

name: Hanno's periplus down West Africa
who: Hanno the Navigator, for Carthage
why: Known from one Greek text said to translate a Punic tablet. Most attempts to place its stops have failed: Harden reports a consensus that he reached at least Senegal, others take him to Cameroon or Gabon, and Mauny thought no further than southern Morocco.
return_note: The text ends abruptly when supplies ran out and does not describe the voyage home, but it presents itself as a report dedicated in a Carthaginian temple.
articles: Hanno the Navigator#Expedition; Hanno the Navigator#Summary

name: Pytheas to Britain and Thule
who: Pytheas of Massalia
why: His own book is lost, but he is quoted by name in at least 39 fragments of later writers, from Hipparchus to Pliny and Strabo, and his measurements of latitude and tides are taken seriously. Where Thule lay, and how far he went into the Baltic, are still argued over.
evidence: fragments in later authors; astronomical observations
return_note: He returned to write On the Ocean; his return route may have run along the coast of Germany.
articles: Pytheas#Circumstances of the voyage; Pytheas#Thule; Pytheas#Discovery of the Baltic

name: Xu Fu and the elixir of life
who: Xu Fu, court sorcerer to Qin Shi Huang
dates_text: first voyage 219 BC; final voyage 210 BC
why: The Records of the Grand Historian record that he sailed to find the immortals and never came back, but not where he went. The story that he landed in Japan first appears more than 1,100 years later, with the monk Yichu; scholars find it inconsistent and unsupported.
return_note: He sailed in 210 BC and never returned; the Shiji says he made himself king of a land of plains and marshes.

name: Zhang Qian's mission to the Yuezhi
who: Zhang Qian, Han envoy, with the guide Ganfu
why: Told in two official histories, the Shiji of Sima Qian (written within living memory) and the Book of Han. Its consequences are documented independently: Han missions to Ferghana and Parthia, and trade with Persia, followed his report.
return_note: Of just over a hundred men, only Zhang Qian and Ganfu returned; he was captured by the Xiongnu twice.

name: The 'lost legion' of Liqian
who: Roman prisoners taken at Carrhae (hypothesis of Homer Dubs, 1941)
why: That Parthia sent about 10,000 Roman prisoners to Margiana is recorded; that some fought for Zhizhi and founded Liqian in China is Dubs's speculation, which historians have not accepted. A 2005 DNA test did not support it.
return_note: No source says any of the prisoners came home; the eastward leg beyond Margiana is a modern hypothesis.

name: Gan Ying's mission towards Rome
who: Gan Ying, sent by the Han general Ban Chao
why: One good written source, the Book of the Later Han, which says he reached Tiaozhi (Characene) by a great sea and was talked out of crossing it by Parthian sailors. Which sea it was, the Persian Gulf or another, is not certain.
return_note: He turned back at the sea and went home; he is said to have brought an envoy back to Luoyang.

name: The 'Roman embassy' of AD 166
who: Men from Daqin claiming to come from 'Andun' (Antoninus); most likely merchants, not legions or official envoys
region: Indian Ocean and South China Sea
why: Recorded once, in the Book of the Later Han, and never in any Roman source. The arrival itself is credible; who they were is not: historians de Crespigny, Bang and Ball think they were Roman merchants rather than diplomats sent by Marcus Aurelius.
evidence: official chronicle; Roman coins and medallions found in Jiaozhi
return_note: No source says whether they ever got home.

name: Faxian's pilgrimage to India
who: Faxian, Buddhist monk, with nine companions
why: Told in his own Record of the Buddhist Kingdoms, written about 414, which is detailed and widely used to date Indian history. It is one first-hand source; little independent record of the journey survives.
return_note: Some of his companions chose to stay in India; Faxian came home by sea, blown off course to Shandong.

name: Hui Shen and the land of Fusang
who: Hui Shen (Huishen), Buddhist monk from Kabul
why: His report survives in the 7th-century Book of Liang; Fusang lay 20,000 li east of Dahan. The 18th-century idea that Fusang was America was refuted by sinologists such as Bretschneider, Laufer and Cordier; Sakhalin, Kamchatka and the Kurils have also been proposed.
return_note: He came back in 499 and reported to the Liang emperor.

name: St Brendan's voyage
who: Saint Brendan of Clonfert and his monks
dates_text: 6th century; the Navigatio was written down about AD 900
why: The Navigatio Sancti Brendani, written about 900, is a Christian wonder tale with a giant fish mistaken for an island. Its 'crystal pillars' and fiery islands may echo icebergs and Iceland, but there is no reliable evidence he reached Greenland or America. Tim Severin showed in 1978 that a leather boat could.
return_note: In the story he returns to Ireland after seven years.
articles: Saint Brendan#The Voyage of Saint Brendan the Abbot; Saint Brendan#Tale of reaching North America

name: Xuanzang's journey to the West
who: Xuanzang, Buddhist monk
why: Several records agree: the travelogue he recited to his monks, three biographies by his collaborators, the 657 Sanskrit texts he brought back and translated, and Tang imperial steles at the Giant Wild Goose Pagoda. The start date (627 or 629) is the main doubt.
evidence: first-hand account; biographies; objects brought back; imperial inscriptions
return_note: Back in Chang'an in 645 with over six hundred texts.

name: Ibn Fadlan's embassy to the Volga Bulgars
who: Ahmad ibn Fadlan, secretary to the caliph's embassy
dates_text: left Baghdad 21 June 921; reached the Bulgar capital 12 May 922
why: His own report (risala) survives in a 13th-century manuscript found at Mashhad in 1923 and in quotations by Yaqut. It is first-hand and precise about dates, but there is no other independent record of the embassy.
return_note: The manuscript breaks off while describing the Khazars. Yaqut claims Ibn Fadlan described his return to Baghdad but quotes none of it.
articles: Ibn Fadlan#The embassy; Ibn Fadlan#Manuscript tradition

name: Bjarni Herjolfsson sights America
who: Bjarni Herjolfsson, Icelandic merchant captain
why: Only the Saga of the Greenlanders, written down around 1200, tells his story; the Saga of Erik the Red instead has Leif find the new land after being blown off course. That he sighted Newfoundland, Labrador and Baffin Island is Oleson's reconstruction.
return_note: He settled with his father in Greenland and later sailed back to Norway.
articles: Bjarni Herjólfsson#Sighting of the American coastline; Leif Erikson#Account in the Saga of Erik the Red

name: Leif Erikson to Vinland
who: Leif Erikson and about 35 crew
why: That Norse crews crossed to North America is proven by archaeology: L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland has Norse buildings, and wood there was cut in 1021. That Leif led the first landing rests on two sagas written about two centuries later, which disagree in detail.
return_note: He sailed home to Greenland and became its chieftain.
articles: Leif Erikson#Discovering Vinland; L'Anse aux Meadows

name: Thorfinn Karlsefni and Gudrid settle Vinland
who: Thorfinn Karlsefni, Gudrid Thorbjarnardottir and 60 to 140 settlers
dates_text: about 1005 to 1008; abandoned in the summer of about 1006 to 1008
why: Both Vinland sagas tell it, at length and with differences (60 men and five women in one, three ships and 140 people in the other). Their son Snorri, born in Vinland, heads Icelandic genealogies. No find names them, though L'Anse aux Meadows may have been their camp and butternuts there show Norse went further south.
return_note: Karlsefni and Gudrid reached Greenland and later Iceland; in the Greenlanders' saga many settlers drowned when one ship was wrecked.
articles: Thorfinn Karlsefni#Vinland; Gudrid Thorbjarnardóttir#Biography; L'Anse aux Meadows

name: Gudrid's pilgrimage to Rome
who: Gudrid Thorbjarnardottir, 'the far-travelled'
dates_text: after her son Snorri married; the year is not recorded
why: One saga, the Saga of the Greenlanders, says she went south to Rome as a widow and came back to live as a nun at the church her son built. Nothing outside the saga confirms it, and talk of her meeting the Pope has no basis.
return_note: She came back from Rome to Iceland and lived as an anchoress.

name: Kupe finds Aotearoa
who: Kupe, with Kuramarotini and a crew of the waka Matawhaorua
dates_text: dates range from 925 to 'never'; historians by 2005 favoured about 1180
why: Kupe lives in Maori oral history, which differs between iwi; his genealogical date has been put anywhere from AD 925 to never (Orbell thought him wholly mythical). The Polynesian settlement of New Zealand itself is not in doubt.
return_note: Tradition says he stayed up to 20 years, then sailed home to Hawaiki from Hokianga, vowing never to return.
articles: Kupe#Voyage to New Zealand; Kupe#Time of arrival

name: Polynesians and South America
who: Unknown Polynesian voyagers (or Native Americans travelling west)
dates_text: contact dated by genetics to about 1150 to 1230; sweet potato in the Cook Islands by about 1000
why: Contact is now widely accepted on independent lines of evidence: the American sweet potato in Polynesia before Europeans, and Native American DNA in eastern Polynesians (Ioannidis and others, Nature 2020). But who sailed, where, and in which direction is argued over, and the pre-Columbian chickens in Chile are contested.
return_note: If Polynesians carried the sweet potato home, someone made the return trip; nobody knows who.
articles: Polynesian navigation#Pre-Columbian contact with the Americas

name: Prince Madoc sails west
who: Madoc ab Owain Gwynedd, a legendary Welsh prince
why: Only allusions survive from medieval tradition; the full story appears in Elizabethan writers (Dee, Peckham, Powel) arguing for an English claim to America. No archaeological, linguistic or other evidence of Madoc has been found.
return_note: Versions disagree: one has him never return, another has him come back to Wales for more settlers.

name: Carpine's embassy to the Great Khan
who: Giovanni da Pian del Carpine and Benedict of Poland
why: Several independent records: Carpine's own book, a separate Relatio by his companion Benedict of Poland, and the reply of Guyuk Khan to Pope Innocent IV, which he carried home. Dates are precise: he rode some 3,000 miles to the Khan's camp in 106 days.
return_note: Reached Kiev on 10 June 1247 and delivered the Khan's letter to the Pope at Lyon.
stated_km_note: an estimated 3,000 miles in 106 days (Batu's camp to Sira Orda)

name: William of Rubruck to Karakorum
who: William of Rubruck, Franciscan friar sent by Louis IX
why: His long report to Louis IX survives in several manuscripts and is precise and vivid, but it is the only full source for the journey.
return_note: Reached the County of Tripoli on 15 August 1255.
articles: William of Rubruck#Mission; William of Rubruck#Travels

name: Marco Polo to the court of Kublai Khan
who: Marco Polo with his father Niccolo and uncle Maffeo
why: One book, dictated in a Genoese prison to Rustichello. Frances Wood (1995) argued he may never have gone beyond Persia, but details he gives (paper money, salt revenues, the Nestorian churches of Zhenjiang, Princess Kokochin's escort) are confirmed by independent Chinese and Persian sources, so most historians accept he reached China.
evidence: first-hand account; independent corroboration of details
return_note: All three Polos came home; of the 600 passengers in Kokochin's convoy only 18 survived.
articles: Marco Polo#Early life and Asian travel; Marco Polo#Authenticity and veracity; Marco Polo#Role of Rustichello

name: Rabban Bar Sauma, from Beijing to Bordeaux
who: Rabban Bar Sauma, Uyghur monk and Mongol envoy
dates_text: left China about 1275; embassy to Europe 1287 to 1288
why: His own account survives in Syriac, and the people he met are on record: Pope Nicholas IV, Philip IV and Edward I. Arghun's 1289 letter to Philip IV, now in the French National Archives, mentions him.
evidence: first-hand account; surviving diplomatic letter; European records
return_note: He came back to Baghdad in 1288 with letters and gifts, but never saw China again.
articles: Rabban Bar Sauma#Pilgrimage to Jerusalem; Rabban Bar Sauma#Ambassador to Europe

name: The Atlantic fleet of Mali ('Abu Bakr II')
who: Mansa Musa's predecessor (popularly but wrongly called Abu Bakr II)
why: One second-hand source: al-Umari recorded what an Egyptian official heard Musa say in Cairo in 1324. It is absent from other Arab historians and from West African oral tradition. Several historians take the voyage seriously, but there is no evidence it reached America.
return_note: By Musa's account the mansa's fleet never returned; that is how Musa became king.
articles: Abu Bakr II#Musa's account; Abu Bakr II#Interpretation; Abu Bakr II#Identity of Musa's predecessor

name: Ibn Battuta's great journey
who: Ibn Battuta of Tangier
region: Africa, Asia and the Indian Ocean
dates_text: 14 June 1325 to 1349 (later trips to Spain and Mali to 1354)
why: One long book, the Rihla, dictated years later from memory. Much is confirmed by fieldwork and other sources, but parts are doubted or borrowed: the trip to Bolghar, Sanaa and the Anatolian loop are questioned, and some scholars think his China chapters lean on earlier writers.
return_note: Back in Morocco in 1349, nearly a quarter of a century after he left.
stated_km_note: totalling around 117,000 km (all his travels to 1354)

name: Zheng He's fifth voyage, to Arabia and East Africa
who: Zheng He and the Ming treasure fleet
why: Recorded in Ming court records, in the accounts of Ma Huan and others, and on a Ming tablet at Quanzhou dated 31 May 1417. Chinese porcelain of the period has been dug up at the East African ports the fleet visited, and a Yemeni source records the ships at Aden in January 1419.
evidence: official chronicle; inscriptions; archaeology; independent foreign record
return_note: The fleet was back in China on 8 August 1419 with envoys, giraffes, zebras and lions.

name: Zheng He's seventh voyage, to Hormuz
who: Zheng He, Wang Jinghong and the treasure fleet
why: A dated itinerary survives, giving the fleet's arrival and departure at every main port; Ma Huan and Fei Xin wrote first-hand accounts, Hong Bao's tomb inscription confirms the squadron's visit to Mecca, and envoys from 11 countries reached court with the fleet.
evidence: official itinerary; first-hand accounts; envoys recorded at court
return_note: The fleet reached Beijing on 22 July 1433.

name: The '1421' claim: China discovers America
who: The Ming fleets, according to Gavin Menzies (2002)
why: Menzies claimed Zheng He's captains reached America, Australia and Antarctica and sailed round the world. Historians reject the book as pseudohistory: it offers no supporting references for any Chinese voyage beyond East Africa, which professional historians accept as the fleet's limit.
return_note: Menzies argued the records were destroyed; there is nothing to say who came back, because there is no evidence anyone went.
articles: 1421: The Year China Discovered the World#Publication, claims, and commercial success; 1421: The Year China Discovered the World#Criticism

name: Afanasy Nikitin's 'Journey Beyond Three Seas'
who: Afanasy Nikitin, merchant of Tver
dates_text: 1468 to spring 1475 (Semyonov's dating; earlier scholars said 1466 to 1472)
why: His own travel notes, taken to Moscow after his death and copied into state chronicles, are first-hand and widely trusted for 15th-century India. They are the only source, and even the dates are debated.
return_note: He died near Smolensk in spring 1475 on the way home to Tver; other merchants carried his notes to Moscow.

name: Columbus's first voyage
who: Christopher Columbus with the Santa Maria, Pinta and Nina
why: His logbook (abstracted by Las Casas), letters, royal documents and many later witnesses agree on the voyage; the landfall island Guanahani is the one real doubt (modern San Salvador is the most likely candidate).
return_note: The Santa Maria was wrecked; 39 men were left at La Navidad on Hispaniola and none were found alive when he came back in 1493.
articles: Voyages of Christopher Columbus#First voyage (1492–1493); Voyages of Christopher Columbus#First return

name: Vasco da Gama's sea route to India
who: Vasco da Gama with four ships and about 170 men
dates_text: 8 July 1497 to 10 July 1499 (Berrio); da Gama himself late August or September 1499
why: A shipboard diary (the Roteiro), King Manuel's letters of July and August 1499, Girolamo Sernigi's letters and Portuguese chronicles all record it; the pillar he set up at Malindi still stands.
evidence: shipboard diary; letters; chronicles; standing monument
return_note: About 55 of roughly 170 men came home; two ships were lost, the Sao Rafael scuttled for lack of crew.
stated_km_note: the distance around Africa to India and back was greater than the length of the equator

name: Magellan and Elcano round the world
who: Ferdinand Magellan, then Juan Sebastian Elcano, with five ships and about 270 men
why: Antonio Pigafetta's journal, the pilots' logs, official inquiries in Spain and Portuguese records describe it in detail; the Victoria's return to Sanlucar is a matter of record.
return_note: 18 men returned with Elcano on the Victoria; Magellan was killed at Mactan in April 1521.

name: Cook's first voyage on the Endeavour
who: James Cook, Joseph Banks and 94 people on HMS Endeavour
why: Cook's journal, Banks's journal and the Admiralty's own instructions and records survive, and the journals were published soon after the return.
return_note: Seven died at Batavia and 23 more on the passage home, among them Tupaia, Green and Parkinson.
articles: First voyage of James Cook#Voyage from Plymouth to Tahiti; First voyage of James Cook#Homeward voyage

name: La Perouse's lost expedition
who: Jean-Francois de La Perouse and 220 men on the Boussole and Astrolabe
why: Journals sent home from Kamchatka and Botany Bay, the British First Fleet's meeting with him at Botany Bay, and the wreckage found at Vanikoro by Peter Dillon in 1826 and by later expeditions.
evidence: journals sent home; foreign records; wrecks found
return_note: Both ships were wrecked at Vanikoro; none of the crews came home. Barthelemy de Lesseps had left at Kamchatka with the journals and crossed Siberia to France.
articles: Lapérouse expedition#Voyage itinerary; Lapérouse expedition#Discovery of the expedition

name: Franklin's lost expedition
who: Sir John Franklin and 129 men on HMS Erebus and HMS Terror
why: The Victory Point note, Inuit testimony, graves on Beechey Island and King William Island, and the wrecks of Erebus (found 2014) and Terror (found 2016) establish where they went and how they died.
evidence: written note found; archaeology; wrecks found; Inuit testimony
return_note: None of the 129 came back; Franklin died on 11 June 1847 and the survivors abandoned the ships in April 1848.

name: Burke and Wills cross Australia
who: Robert O'Hara Burke, William John Wills and 17 others
why: Brahe's buried letter at the Dig Tree, the reports of several relief expeditions, the official records and the survivor John King's testimony all agree; the Dig Tree still stands on Cooper Creek.
evidence: field notebooks; official inquiry; survivor testimony
return_note: Seven men died; of the four who reached the Gulf, only John King came back alive to Melbourne.
stated_km_note: Melbourne to the Gulf of Carpentaria, around 3,250 km (one way)

name: Amundsen's march to the South Pole
who: Roald Amundsen and four companions with 52 dogs
why: Amundsen's own account and telegrams from Hobart, and physical proof found by rivals: the tent Polheim, with a letter for King Haakon, was found by Scott's party a month later.
evidence: diaries; physical evidence found by others
return_note: All five men returned to Framheim on 25 January 1912, with 11 of the 52 dogs.

name: Scott's polar party
who: Robert Falcon Scott, Edward Wilson, Henry Bowers, Lawrence Oates and Edgar Evans
why: Scott's diary and the bodies, tent and records found by the search party in November 1912, plus the diaries of the support parties who turned back.
return_note: All five died on the way back: Evans on 17 February, Oates in mid March, and the last three about 29 March, 11 miles short of One Ton Depot.
articles: Terra Nova Expedition#South polar journey; Terra Nova Expedition#The last march; Terra Nova Expedition#Eleven miles

name: Shackleton's Endurance and the return
who: Ernest Shackleton and the 28 men of the Weddell Sea party
why: Shackleton's own account, Hurley's photographs, witnesses at the whaling stations on South Georgia, the Chilean rescue by the Yelcho, and the wreck of Endurance, found on the Weddell Sea floor in 2022.
return_note: All 28 men of the Endurance party came home. (The Ross Sea party on the far side lost three men.)

name: Kon-Tiki, the raft that tested the wrong theory
who: Thor Heyerdahl and five companions
why: A filmed and logged modern voyage. It proved a balsa raft could drift from Peru to Polynesia; it did not prove that anyone did, and Heyerdahl's theory of American origins for Polynesians is not accepted.
return_note: All six men survived the wreck on Raroia reef and were taken to Tahiti.
